rationale: B wins because it has the discipline to stop at three real press shapes and make the agency MOU conditional instead of decorating the update into a category story. Its best line, "A state fire agency signed an MOU with a satellite startup that hasn't launched anything," is the cleanest journalist hook in either set. A is strong, but "The Race to Spot a Wildfire From Space Before It Becomes a Disaster" overreaches into a "category shift" from one pre-launch company. That's the kind of smart-sounding angle that gets a founder into trouble on email two.
gaps_in_A: "commercial small-sat constellations dedicated to a single public-safety function" turns one company into a category without outside evidence. A later refused angle says "One company is a data point, not a trend," which undercuts this angle directly.

"The prevailing assumption is that fire and public-safety agencies require demonstrated, operational capability" may be true, but it is not in the update. It needs to be framed as a question, not a premise.

"The Race to Spot a Wildfire From Space Before It Becomes a Disaster" is the weakest headline because Helio has no satellite in orbit and no operational results. It risks sounding like capability, not ambition.
gaps_in_B: "an honest answer on why they left" is not proof the founder-profile angle needs. It invites biography gossip when the real proof is role, tenure, and technical transfer.
"Story type: trend" on the MOU angle is mislabeled. This is a contrarian procurement/buyer story, not a trend unless there are other agencies or startups in evidence.
"buyer/regulator protagonist" is sloppy. A state fire agency may be a buyer or operating partner; regulator is not established by the update.
It does not explicitly ask whether the founders can be named in the uncomfortable questions. The founder-profile angle cannot move without names and tenure confirmation.
